extracted.intended_audience: regulated entities, environmental and industry stakeholders, and attorneys participating in EPA rulemaking under Clean Air Act section 111
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and legal standards the EPA uses when determining the Best System of Emission Reduction (BSER) and setting standards of performance under Clean Air Act section 111, including factors to consider, allowable scope of systems, treatment of developing technologies, and judicial review standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory factors in 'adequately demonstrated' / BSER determination
rubrics_metrics.description: CAA section 111(a)(1)'s enumerated factors are part of the 'adequately demonstrated' determination and may be considered when determining which system of emission reduction is the 'best.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The preamble states that the statutory text at CAA section 111(a)(1) by its terms lists factors that are part of the 'adequately demonstrated' determination; the D.C. Circuit's caselaw makes clear EPA may consider these same factors (cost, energy, and environmental impacts) when determining the BSER. See Sierra Club v. Costle, 657 F.2d at 330. (Surrounding discussion cites that EPA can weigh cost, energy, and environmental impacts.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Explicit factors to weigh: cost, energy, and environmental impacts
rubrics_metrics.description: When assessing whether a system is adequately demonstrated or the 'best,' EPA should take into account cost of compliance, non-air-quality health and environmental impact, and energy considerations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The preamble quotes statutory and legislative language (e.g., 42 U.S.C. 7419(b)(3) and committee reports) emphasizing cost, nonair quality health and environmental impact, and energy consideration. EPA may exercise judgment on the weight of these elements; legislative history supports considering economic practicability alongside environmental protection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition and use of subcategories tied to BSER-relevant characteristics
rubrics_metrics.description: Subcategories may be established based on characteristics relevant to the BSER, and those characteristics can differ between new and existing sources.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites 40 CFR 60.22(b)(5) and 60.22a(b)(5): 'Because the definition of subcategories depends on characteristics relevant to the BSER ... the EPA may establish different subcategories as between new and existing sources.' Guidance implies careful, contextual subcategorization tied to the technical/operational features that affect applicability of controls.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three-step analysis for setting a standard of performance
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA should apply the three-step analysis (as described in prior NSPS rulemakings) when setting a standard of performance under section 111.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The preamble references the 'three-step analysis' used in prior rulemakings (e.g., Oil and Natural Gas Sector NSPS and others) as descriptive of the approach for setting standards. Although the steps are not enumerated in this excerpt, the citation signals that rulemaking should follow the established multi-step analytical framework used in prior section 111 actions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Permissibility of extrapolation/projection from limited testing or early deployments
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA may determine a system of emission reduction to be 'adequately demonstrated' based on some amount of projection or extrapolation from testing results even if aspects of the system are still in development.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The preamble notes that EPA may extrapolate from testing results (citing Sierra Club v. Costle) rather than relying only on consistent, widespread performance, and that EPA has in past relied on technologies used extensively abroad or in limited U.S. use. This supports considering emerging or pilot technologies when justified by data.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allowance for lead time where projected technologies are used
rubrics_metrics.description: When projecting technology development into future performance, EPA may provide 'lead time' to accommodate the development and deployment of projected technologies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The preamble explains that authorizing lead time accommodates projected technology development and cites further discussion in section VIII.F. This is guidance for timing and implementation schedules tied to BSER-based standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope of 'system of emission reduction' can be broader than measures applied at each source
rubrics_metrics.description: The BSER need not be limited to control measures that could be applied at and to each source; EPA has rejected an interpretation requiring that BSER measures be applied at each individual source.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The preamble recounts the ACE Rule's prior narrow interpretation (limiting BSER to measures applied at each source) and notes EPA subsequently rejected that interpretation as too narrow (citing Adoption and Submittal of State Plans... 88 FR 80535). This permits consideration of broader systems-level approaches in selecting BSER.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cost reasonableness constraint (costs not 'exorbitant' or fatal to industry survival)
rubrics_metrics.description: While costs are a factor, the EPA should avoid standards whose costs are 'exorbitant' or 'greater than the industry could bear and survive.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The preamble cites case law (e.g., Lignite Energy Council; Portland Cement Ass'n v. EPA) and legislative history expressing that costs should not be so high as to be exorbitant or to threaten industry survival. Courts have allowed deference to EPA's judgments about cost acceptability but expect reasoned balancing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Administrator discretion in weighing statutory elements
rubrics_metrics.description: Because Congress did not assign specific weights to the statutory elements, the Administrator has discretion to exercise judgment in how much weight to give each factor in promulgating standards.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites New York v. Reilly and related authority that 'Because Congress did not assign the specific weight the Administrator should accord each of these factors, the Administrator is free to exercise his discretion.' This indicates evaluative flexibility but requires reasoned explanation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deferential judicial standard of review requiring reasoned decision-making
rubrics_metrics.description: Judicial review of EPA standards is appropriately deferential; courts will affirm EPA actions unless they are arbitrary, capricious, an abuse of discretion, or otherwise not in accordance with law, but will require that standards be the result of reasoned decision-making.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The preamble cites Nat'l Asphalt Pavement Ass'n v. Train and Ethyl Corp. v. EPA to explain that courts give deference in these technical areas but evaluate whether EPA's standards resulted from reasoned decision-making. This is a reminder to document and justify analytic choices in the rulemaking record.
